title: Active seizure - protect and reassure

source.name: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines 2021 - First Aid, seizures

medical_disclaimer: This protocol has not been reviewed by a clinician and is not a substitute for professional medical care. It is intended to support a bystander while emergency services are being contacted.

escalation_rules.reason: A seizure lasting five minutes or longer needs emergency treatment immediately.
More than one seizure in a short period needs emergency treatment.

steps.instruction: Move hard or sharp objects away from around the person and protect their head. Do not hold them down and do not put anything in their mouth.
steps.question: Have you cleared the area around them, and are they on their side?

steps.instruction: Call the emergency number and say the person is having a seizure and how long it has lasted. Give your exact location and stay on the line.
steps.question: Have you called, how long has the seizure lasted, and what is your exact location?

fact_questions.caller_location: Are you with the person right now?
fact_questions.seizure_duration_minutes: Roughly how long has the seizure been going on?

steps.instruction: Note the time the seizure started. Stay close, speak calmly, and time how long the seizure lasts.
steps.question: What time did the seizure start, and how long has it lasted?

steps.instruction: When the seizure stops, roll the person onto their side so that anything from the stomach can drain out of the mouth. Keep their airway clear.
steps.question: Are they breathing, and are they on their side?

transitions.note: The person is not breathing normally after the seizure. Emergency treatment and chest compressions are needed now.

steps.instruction: Stay with the person while they recover. Do not give them anything to eat or drink until they are fully awake. Tell the ambulance crew how long the seizure lasted.
steps.question: Are they recovering, and has the ambulance crew taken over?
